# Compound

> A personal self-development app. People learn in **topics** (skills with steps to tick, resources, projects), keep **lists** (books to read, films to watch…), plan **routines** for Today, save notes, ideas and links in a **notebook**, and keep **habits** on Wellbeing. You can read and build all of this for the user through the API or the MCP server.

## Connect

- MCP server (streamable HTTP): `/mcp` with the header `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. If you can't set headers, use `/mcp/<token>`.
- REST API: `/api/v1` with the same header. Description: `/api/v1/openapi.json`.
- The user makes the token in the app: Settings → AI access. It can read, add and change their data, but never delete it. Still, never show it back to them or put it anywhere else.

Tools (MCP) and routes (REST) are the same operations:

| Tool | REST |
| --- | --- |
| list_topics, get_topic | GET /topics, GET /topics/{id} |
| create_topic, update_topic | POST /topics, PATCH /topics/{id} |
| list_lists, get_list | GET /lists, GET /lists/{id} |
| create_list, update_list | POST /lists, PATCH /lists/{id} |
| list_routines, add_routine | GET /routines, POST /routines |
| list_notes, add_note | GET /notes, POST /notes |
| list_habits | GET /habits |
| get_focus, set_focus | GET /focus, PUT /focus |

Before changing anything, look at what's there (`list_topics`, `list_lists`) so you don't make a duplicate.

## A good topic

A topic is one area someone wants to get good at: "English", "System design", "Personal finance". It has no dates inside: what's next is always the first step not yet ticked, so a slow week never puts anyone behind a schedule.

- **name**: short, it shows on tags and buttons. One or two words.
- **description** (About): 2–4 short paragraphs, separated by an empty line. What this area is, why it matters for this person, and how to approach it (the order, how much a week, what to skip).
- **goals**: 2–4 outcomes in plain words, where the person will be at the end. "Explain a system design trade-off in an interview", not "Learn system design".
- **months**: optional target duration. Leave it out unless the person gave one.
- **skills**, in the order to learn them. 3–7 skills per topic. Each skill:
  - **name**: the skill, e.g. "Caching".
  - **intro**: one or two sentences, what it is and why it matters.
  - **steps**: 3–10 concrete steps, in order, each small enough to learn in one or two sessions: "Cache-aside vs write-through", "Cache invalidation and TTLs". Not "Learn caching".
- **resources**: the best few, not everything. 5–15 per topic. Each has a **title**, a **url** (only a link you checked, see Finding resources. Leave it out otherwise), a **kind** (book, course, video, article, podcast, tool, doc, practice, other), a one-line **note** on why it's worth it, and **free** if it costs nothing. Prefer free, current and widely recommended.
- **projects**: 2–5 things to build or do that use the skills, from small to big. Each has a **name**, a **goal**, a few **steps**, **done** (how to know it's finished), **trains** (the skill names it practises) and a **size**: small (a few hours to a few days), medium (one to a few weeks) or big (a month or more). Codes like EN1, EN2 are given automatically.

Write in the user's language (the app is in English and Ukrainian), plain and friendly. Short sentences. Never use semicolons.

## Preparing a topic, step by step

1. **Look first.** `list_topics`: if a topic for this area exists, improve it with `update_topic` instead of making a second one.
2. **Ask before you build**, in one short message, only what you can't guess:
   - Their level now (never touched it, some basics, use it at work).
   - What they want to be able to do, and by when (that becomes **goals** and, if they give a date, **months**).
   - Time per week (sets how big steps and projects can be).
   - Free only, or paid is fine. Books, video, courses, hands-on: what they like.
   - The language they learn best in.
3. **Outline the skills.** Foundations first, then what builds on them. Each skill should be learnable in one to three weeks at their pace. If a skill needs more, split it.
4. **Break each skill into steps** that fit one or two sessions and say exactly what to learn or do: "Write three sentences with the present perfect about your week", not "Grammar".
5. **Find resources** for the skills (see below), at least one per skill, the best ones first.
6. **Design projects** that use several skills, from a small win in the first weeks to one bigger piece at the end. A project should produce something they can show or use.
7. **Show the plan** as a short outline (skills with their steps, the resources, the projects) and ask if it fits. Then create it with one `create_topic` call.
8. **Offer the next move**, don't just do it: `set_focus` to make it the focus topic, or `add_routine` for a daily habit ("20 minutes of English", weekdays).

## Finding resources

- **Search, don't recall.** If you can browse or search the web, use it: find candidates, open them, and check the page is live, matches the title, and is current. Never invent or guess a URL. If you can't check a link, leave `url` out and keep the title, so the user can find it.
- **Where good resources usually are:**
  - The official docs or guide of the tool or field (the language's own tutorial, the framework's docs).
  - Well-known free courses: university open courseware (MIT OpenCourseWare, Stanford Online), freeCodeCamp, The Odin Project, Khan Academy, CS50, Coursera or edX courses that can be audited.
  - Classic books the field agrees on, with the author in the note.
  - Long-running YouTube channels or playlists from practitioners, not one-off videos.
  - Practice sites with feedback (exercises, katas, language exchange).
- **Choose like a good teacher:** a few great ones beat a long list. Prefer free, current (check the year for anything technical), widely recommended, and in the user's language when one exists. Mix kinds: something to read, something to watch, something to practise.
- **Write the note as a reason:** what it covers and when to use it ("The clearest intro to caching. Read before the Caching skill."), not "Great resource".
- **Prefer stable links:** the course or book page, a playlist, the docs section, over a deep link that will move.

## Best practices

- **Concrete over vague.** Every step and goal should be checkable: you can tell when it's done.
- **Small steps.** Many small steps keep progress visible: the app shows the next unticked step on Today.
- **Order matters.** Skills, steps and projects are done in the order you give. Put what unlocks the rest first.
- **Fewer, better resources.** 5–15 per topic. Remove duplicates that teach the same thing.
- **Projects make it stick.** Each topic needs at least one small project early, so learning turns into doing.
- **Cross links.** Text can mention project codes (EN1) and they become links in the app. Keep codes exactly as written.
- **Don't overwrite their work.** When updating, get the topic first and send ids back. Nothing you leave out is removed, but text you send replaces the old text.
- **Be honest about size.** If the goal and time don't fit (fluent Japanese in a month at 2 hours a week), say so and suggest a goal that does.

## A good list

A list is a set of things to get through: "100 films everyone should watch", "50 sci-fi books".

- **name**: short, may start with an emoji: "🎬 Films".
- **title**: the full title: "100 films everyone should watch".
- **detail_label**: what the small line under each item is: "Year", "Author", "Artist", "Country".
- **items**: each with a **title** and a **detail** ("1972"). Real, well-known items only, best first or in a sensible order.
- Check titles and details (year, author) against a reliable source if you can search. Use the title the user would recognise in their language, with the original in the detail if it helps ("Spirited Away", detail "2001, Hayao Miyazaki").
- `list_lists` first: if a similar list exists, add to it with `update_list` instead of making a new one.

## Other things you can add

- **Routines** (Today): `add_routine` with a title, optional details, a topic id, and when: `"daily"`, `{ "kind": "weekly", "days": ["mon", "thu"] }`, `{ "kind": "monthly", "day": 1 }` (or -1 for the last day) or `{ "kind": "once", "date": "YYYY-MM-DD" }`. They count for the streak unless `counts_for_streak` is false.
- **Notes**: `add_note` with text, an optional url (makes it a link) and tags (the tag `idea` makes it an idea).
- **Focus**: one learning topic is the focus. Today shows its next step, its current project and its next resource. `set_focus` changes it.

## Updating

`update_topic` and `update_list` change only the fields you send. In a list you send (skills, resources, projects, goals, a skill's steps, items), items with an id that exists are changed, new ones are added, and items you leave out stay where they are, after the ones you sent. Get the topic or list first and keep the ids so ticks and notes stay on the right items. Sending items in a new order reorders them.

Nothing can be deleted through the API or MCP: there are no delete tools, and updates never remove items. If something should go, tell the user to remove it in the app (Edit, then the red minus).

## Example: create_topic

```json
{
  "name": "English",
  "description": "Clear spoken English for work: meetings, calls and presentations.\n\nAim to be understood the first time, not for a perfect accent. Twenty minutes a day beats two hours on Sunday.",
  "goals": ["Lead a meeting in English without notes", "People rarely ask you to repeat yourself"],
  "skills": [
    { "name": "Pronunciation", "intro": "The sounds and rhythm that make you easy to understand.", "steps": ["The sounds that differ from your language", "Word stress", "Sentence rhythm and intonation"] },
    { "name": "Speaking at work", "intro": "Phrases and habits for meetings and calls.", "steps": ["Opening and closing a meeting", "Disagreeing politely", "Asking someone to repeat or slow down"] }
  ],
  "resources": [
    { "title": "YouGlish", "url": "https://youglish.com", "kind": "tool", "note": "Hear any word said by native speakers in real videos.", "free": true }
  ],
  "projects": [
    { "name": "Record yourself before and after", "goal": "Record the same 2-minute text today and again in 3 months.", "steps": ["Pick a 2-minute text", "Record it today", "Record it again in 3 months and compare"], "done": "Two recordings, and you can hear the difference.", "trains": ["Pronunciation"], "size": "small" }
  ]
}
```
